newsitem.title: FRANCE: Communist beats far-rightist in French by-election.
newsitem.headline: Communist beats far-rightist in French by-election.

text.p: A Communist beat a far-right candidate on Sunday in a bitter parliamentary by-election that reflected deep doubts in France about European Union integration and mainstream politics.

Roger Mei won 60.32 percent of the vote to 39.68 percent for the National Front's Damien Bariller in the depressed southern coal-mining town of Gardanne, where Mei is mayor, according to final results.
"I've beaten the candidate of hatred and violence," Mei, 61, told reporters after the vote, for which only 49.9 percent of the electorate bothered to turn out.

"The Union of the Rotten has elected the candidate of the Gulag," Bariller, 30, said after parties in the ruling centre-right coalition gave tacit backing to Mei as the lesser of two evils. "The National Front lost with honour."

Candidates for parties from the conservative Gaullist party of Prime Minister Alain Juppe to opposition Socialists, were humiliated last week when they were knocked out in a first round and Mei and Bariller qualified for the run-off.

Both Mei, 61, and Bariller oppose plans for economic and monetary union including a single European currency from 1999. Mainstream parties all favour the EU plan but are struggling to persuade an unenthusiastic electorate of its merits.

The by-election was for the National Assembly seat near the southern port of Marseille left vacant by the resignation of bankrupt businessman and former soccer boss Bernard Tapie, who is battling jail sentences.

National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen, who wants to expel three million immigrants from France, won 15 percent on the first round of last year's presidential elections but Sunday's defeat leaves it with no seats in parliament.
French leaders all show disgust for Le Pen, while seeking ways to woo his voters. Prime Minister Alain Juppe recently described him as "deeply, almost viscerally racist, anti-Semitic and xenophobic".
Tapie's favoured successor, former health and humanitarian action minister Bernard Kouchner also backed by the Socialists, won a dismal 13.29 percent in a vote marred by high abstention.
Communist party boss Robert Hue said that Mei's victory was "a setback for the National Front and for the right. This is an extra snub for Mr Juppe".
